name: Chloe Whitfield
presenting_complaint: Acute breathlessness and wheeze, unable to speak in full sentences

conditions: Two previous ICU admissions for asthma (last intubated 2 years ago)
medical_history.social: University student. Non-smoker. Recent viral upper respiratory tract infection. Lives in share house with a cat.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 24-year-old woman presents to ED with 6 hours of worsening breathlessness, chest tightness and audible wheeze following a viral illness. She can only speak in single words, is using accessory muscles and is sitting forward. She has a history of two ICU admissions for asthma, one requiring intubation. Obs: RR 32, HR 132, SpO2 90% on room air, unable to complete sentences. PEF is less than 40% of predicted.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Onset and duration: 6 hours of progressive breathlessness, wheeze and chest tightness after a viral URTI
Severity markers by history: unable to speak in full sentences (single words only), exhaustion, reliever overuse (2 salbutamol canisters this week)
High-risk asthma history: two prior ICU admissions, previous intubation/ventilation, poor preventer compliance
Trigger and red-flag screen: cat exposure, viral illness; screen for anaphylaxis, pneumothorax and cardiac cause
Medication and allergy history documented, including inhaler technique and preventer adherence
objective: Bedside PEF (peak expiratory flow) and continuous SpO2 with early ABG/VBG for pH and PaCO2
Respiratory exam: air entry, wheeze intensity, accessory muscle use — actively listen for a SILENT CHEST (pre-arrest sign)
Full obs set: RR, HR, SpO2, work of breathing, conscious state, ability to speak
Cardiac monitor and IV access; assess for exhaustion, cyanosis and altered conscious state
Portable CXR only if pneumothorax/consolidation suspected — do NOT send an unstable asthmatic to imaging alone
assessment: Acute severe / life-threatening asthma (SpO2 <92%, unable to speak in sentences, HR >120, PEF <40% predicted, high-risk phenotype)
Recognise silent chest, exhaustion, rising or normalising PaCO2 and bradycardia/hypotension as life-threatening/near-fatal features
Consider differentials: anaphylaxis, pneumothorax, inhaled foreign body, pneumonia, cardiac failure
plan: Sit patient upright and give high-flow oxygen titrated to SpO2 94-98% (FIRST action)
Continuous / back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg driven by oxygen (repeat continuously) PLUS ipratropium bromide 500 microgram nebulised
Systemic corticosteroid early: prednisolone 50 mg orally OR hydrocortisone 100 mg IV if unable to swallow
IV magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 minutes for life-threatening/severe asthma not responding
IV access x2, obtain ABG/VBG for pH and PaCO2, and place on continuous cardiac and SpO2 monitoring
Escalate early: call ED consultant and ICU/anaesthetics for life-threatening features; prepare for IV salbutamol/aminophylline and possible intubation/ventilation
Reassess response with serial PEF, obs and repeat ABG; do NOT discharge — admit, and arrange HDU/ICU if not improving

critical_errors: Interpreting a silent chest, exhaustion, or a normalising/rising PaCO2 as reassurance — these are pre-arrest signs, not improvement; failing to escalate is the make-or-break error
Discharging or sending the patient home too early after apparent improvement without admission and observation
Sending an unstable severe asthmatic to imaging (CXR/CT) unaccompanied instead of resuscitating in a monitored area
Failing to give systemic corticosteroid, or omitting nebulised bronchodilators, in acute severe asthma
must_not_miss: Life-threatening / near-fatal asthma requiring ICU and early senior/anaesthetic involvement
Silent chest and normal/rising PaCO2 recognised as signs of impending respiratory failure
Systemic steroids and continuous bronchodilators + ipratropium given early, magnesium for non-responders
Tension pneumothorax or anaphylaxis excluded as a cause of acute deterioration
